subject: Archaeology
title: The San José: The Holy Grail of Shipwrecks
description: Learn The San José: The Holy Grail of Shipwrecks in one minute.

hook.text: A Spanish galleon carrying $17 billion in gold sank off Colombia in 1708. Three countries are fighting over it.

buildup.text: The San José was sunk by British warships during the War of Spanish Succession. Its treasure was never recovered.

discovery.text: Colombia announced the wreck's discovery in 2015. Cameras showed cannons, ceramics, and gold coins on the seabed.

twist.text: Spain says the ship is theirs. Colombia says it is in their waters. A U.S. company claims it found it first.

climax.text: The legal battle highlights a global problem: who owns wrecks — the flag state, the coastal nation, or the finder?

punchline.text: Seventeen billion dollars on the seabed. Three countries, zero agreement.

quiz.question: Why is the San José shipwreck legally controversial?
options: It contains human remains that families want left undisturbed
Spain, Colombia, and a U.S. company all claim ownership
UNESCO has declared it off-limits to all salvage operations

details.summary: The San José, a Spanish galleon sunk by the British in 1708 off Colombia, reportedly carried treasure worth billions in gold, silver, and emeralds. Found in 2015, the wreck is at the center of an international legal dispute between Colombia, Spain, indigenous groups, and salvage companies over.
details.whyItMatters: The San José embodies the collision between national sovereignty, colonial heritage, indigenous rights, and commercial treasure hunting. Its legal battle will set precedents for underwater cultural heritage worldwide.
takeaways: The San José sank in 1708 off Colombia carrying immense treasure
Found in 2015, it sparked an international ownership dispute
The legal battle will shape underwater heritage law globally

faq.question: How much is the San José treasure worth?
faq.answer: Estimates range from $4 billion to $20 billion depending on how the gold, silver, and emeralds are valued. The Colombian government declared it national cultural heritage. Spain claims sovereign immunity as the flag state.

faq.question: Who owns the San José legally?
faq.answer: This is actively being disputed. Colombia claims it as part of its underwater cultural patrimony. Spain argues sovereign vessel immunity under international law. A U.S. salvage company claims a prior discovery agreement. Courts in multiple countries have weighed in with conflicting rulings.
